notes.meaning: Amos sings a funeral song over Israel, as if the nation were already dead. It shows how sure the coming judgment is. Matthew Henry notes that we need to hear warning words as well as words of comfort. It is God's word, not only the prophet's.

Israel is pictured as a young woman who was proud of her beauty, strength and wealth. Now she lies thrown down on her own ground, and no one comes to lift her up. The northern kingdom of ten tribes was in fact never set up as a kingdom again.

A town that sends out a thousand soldiers will see only a hundred come home. A town that sends a hundred will get back only ten. Only about one in ten will survive the coming war. Calvin notes that God still keeps a small number alive.

Right after the funeral song, God holds out hope: "Seek Me and live!" Life here means escaping judgment and having real life with God. If they die, it is their own fault, because God is ready to forgive those who turn back.

differ.view: The call to turn back goes out to everyone. But God inwardly draws his chosen ones, and those who refuse are left without excuse.

notes.meaning: Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba had a holy past. God met Jacob at Bethel, Israel camped at Gilgal under Joshua, and Abraham worshipped at Beersheba. Now they had become centers of false worship, like the golden calf at Bethel. Amos makes a play on words: Gilgal will be "rolled away" into exile, and Bethel, "house of God," will become nothing. God is not truly sought unless he is sought alone.

differ.view: God has given his own rule for how he is to be worshipped. Forms of worship that people invent cannot be mixed in, and turning to God means leaving them behind.

notes.meaning: The call is repeated: seek the LORD and live. If they don't, God will sweep like fire through the "house of Joseph." That means the northern kingdom, whose leading tribe, Ephraim, came from Joseph. None of the idols at Bethel will be able to put the fire out.

Justice should taste sweet to people who have been wronged. These leaders and judges turned it into wormwood, a very bitter plant. They threw what is right down on the ground and trampled it, mostly by giving unfair rulings in court.

Amos reminds them who God is. He made the star groups that Amos watched as a shepherd at night. He turns the darkest night into morning and day into night, and he pours the sea's waters on the land, as rain in mercy or as flood in judgment. With the same power he can bring sudden ruin on the strong, and no fortress can stand against him. Older translations read verse 9 as God giving the weak strength against the strong.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think these hymn-like lines, or their order, may have been arranged later. One scholar moved verse 7 to follow verse 9.

notes.meaning: The city gate was where court cases were heard. The people hated anyone who spoke up against wrong there. That might be an honest judge, a truthful witness, or a prophet like Amos. Matthew Henry says they could not stand the sight of an honest man.

The rich trampled the poor and forced loads of grain from them, the very food they needed to live. They built fancy stone houses and planted fine vineyards, but they will never enjoy them. This is the curse Moses warned about in Deuteronomy 28. What is gained dishonestly is not kept for long.

God sees every sin, small and great. The judges were hard on innocent people. They took bribes or "ransom money" to let guilty people go free. They turned the poor away from justice in court because the poor could not pay.

In such evil times, wise people stay quiet. Complaining to corrupt judges does no good, and speaking up can be dangerous. Calvin says they are forced into silence. The prophet himself, though, cannot keep quiet.

"Seek good, not evil, so that you may live." The people boasted that God was always with them because they were his covenant people. A covenant is God's binding promise to his people. But God would truly be with them only if they turned to doing good.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think verses 14 and 15 were probably not in their original place in the chapter.

notes.meaning: They must hate evil, love good, and bring back fair judgment in the courts. "Perhaps" God will be gracious. That word does not mean God is unwilling. It shows how serious things are and urges them to turn back quickly. "Remnant" means only a small number will be spared.

Since they will not turn back, crying will fill every street and square. There will be so many deaths that farmers are called from their fields to help the hired mourners. Even the vineyards, usually places of joy, will be full of weeping. God says, "I will pass through your midst," like the night he passed through Egypt. But this time he will not pass over Israel.

Some Israelites looked forward to "the Day of the LORD," expecting God to crush their enemies and bless them. Others said it mockingly, not believing it would ever come. Amos warns that for sinful Israel it will be darkness, meaning disaster, not light. Christians have also heard here a warning about the final judgment for those who do not repent.

It is like a man who runs from a lion and meets a bear. He escapes into his house, leans on the wall, and a snake bites him. Escaping one disaster only leads to another. No place, inside or outside, is safe for people who refuse to turn back.

Amos says it again, even more strongly: that day will be deep darkness, with no brightness at all. The word for "gloom" is the one used for the plague of darkness in Egypt. There will be no good news in it for those who keep doing evil.

God says he hates their religious feasts and will not "smell" their offerings. In other words, he will not accept them as a pleasing gift. The problem was that their worship covered up a life of sin, and it was a man-made copy of true worship at Bethel. Burnt, grain and peace offerings, even of the best cattle, mean nothing to God without obedience.
Their singing and harp music, copied from the temple worship, was only noise to God, like a heavy load he wanted taken away. Their hearts were not right with him, so he would not listen.

What God wants instead is justice flowing like a river and right living like a stream that never dries up. Justice should run freely and steadily, all year round. It should not be blocked by bribes or fear of powerful people. This is what God desires more than sacrifices.

God reminds them of the forty years in the wilderness. Even then their worship was not given to him alone. They carried around shrines and images of star gods, probably linked to the planet Saturn. Israel in Amos's day was acting just like their ancestors. Stephen quotes these verses in Acts 7:42-43.

So God will send them into exile beyond Damascus. That means to Assyria, a far place from which return was harder. They had been drawn into worshipping idols, so God would send them away among idol-worshippers. He is the "God of Hosts," Lord of the very stars they worshipped. Stephen says "beyond Babylon," which takes in the same distant lands.
